unit.title: Formulate a human resource strategic plan

summary: This unit teaches you to formulate a human resource (HR) strategic plan for a Jamaican ministry, agency or other public body. You will learn how the HR plan grows out of the organisation's corporate plan, how to scan the environment and analyse the workforce, how to forecast the demand for and supply of staff and find the gaps, how to set objectives and choose strategies, how to consult, cost and get approval, and how to implement, monitor and review the plan.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification, with a public-sector code (PSA). It is for HR managers, directors and senior officers in ministries, departments, agencies, statutory bodies, health authorities and municipal corporations. An **HR strategic plan** sets out how the organisation will make sure it has the **right number of people, with the right skills, in the right places, at the right cost** to achieve its goals over the next three to five years.

Without a plan, HR reacts to vacancies and problems as they arise. With a plan, HR looks ahead: it asks what the organisation will need to do, what workforce that requires, what the organisation has now, and how to close the gap.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workplace
rows: Link HR to the corporate plan
Start from the agency's strategic goals and ask what people and skills each goal needs.
Carry out an environmental scan (PESTLE) and SWOT analysis to identify what will affect the workforce.
Build a workforce profile: posts, vacancies, ages, skills, turnover, absence; do a skills audit.
Estimate the staff needed and the staff likely to be available, using ratios, trends and judgement.
Compare demand and supply and say how many people and which skills are missing or surplus.
Write SMART HR objectives; choose strategies for recruitment, retention, development, succession, performance, wellbeing and relations.
Involve stakeholders, cost the plan, prioritise, and obtain the approvals needed.
Plan actions, owners and timelines; manage risk; measure progress; update the plan when things change.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and calculations (vacancy rate, turnover, ratios, gaps, costs, averages).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms and short sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: a workforce and gap analysis for a made-up agency with SWOT and SMART objectives; and drafting the core of an HR plan, consulting a staff representative and presenting it to a senior management panel.

blocks.note: Most questions on this unit follow one chain: corporate goal, then people needed, then people available, then the gap, then the action, then the cost, then the measure. Keep that chain in mind.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Purpose of the plan and link to the corporate plan

blocks.h: What an HR strategic plan does

ul: Makes sure the organisation has the people its goals require.
Moves HR from reacting to planning ahead.
Covers how the organisation will **attract, develop, deploy, reward and keep** its staff, and how it will build a positive working culture.
Gives managers, staff, unions and central approving bodies one agreed picture of the workforce future.
Ties HR actions and budgets to the organisation's goals.

head: Strategic HR issue (this plan)
Day-to-day HR issue (not this plan)
rows: Building digital skills over the next five years
Planning for retirement of senior officers
Filling one clerk's vacancy next week
Redesigning jobs for a new online service
Booking a room for a training session

blocks.h: The link to the corporate (strategic) plan

blocks.p: The HR plan must **grow out of the agency's corporate or strategic plan**. For each strategic goal, such as moving services online or extending services to rural parishes, ask: **what people and skills does this goal need, and what changes in numbers, structure or capability follow?** The HR objectives are then written to support the goals; HR actions and budgets are tied to them.

flow: Study the corporate plan and meet senior managers to understand the goals
For each goal, work out the people implications (numbers, skills, structure, location)
Analyse the environment and the current workforce
Forecast demand and supply; find the gaps
Set HR objectives linked to the goals
Choose strategies and write the implementation plan, costs and risks
Consult, revise and approve
Implement, monitor, report and review

ul: The HR plan should cover the **same period** as the corporate plan (for example four years for a municipal corporation's corporate plan), and be reviewed **yearly**.
Report progress alongside the corporate plan's measures.
If the corporate plan changes, the HR plan changes too.

blocks.p: The head of the body (for example the Permanent Secretary or chief executive) usually gives final approval, after consultation with unions and associations, and agreement from central bodies that approve budgets and posts. New posts cannot be funded without those bodies' approval.

blocks.note: Public bodies work within public service rules: pay and posts are set within central policy, recruitment is on merit and employment law and service rules apply. Check the current rules and approvals when drafting. Parish councils became municipal corporations in 2016, so use that name for local government bodies.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: An **environmental scan** looks outside the organisation (and inside) for changes that will affect its workforce over the plan period. A common checklist is **PESTLE**.

head: Factor
Questions
Example for a public hospital or agency
rows: Government policy, budgets, public service reform, mergers
A decision to merge two agencies; limits on new posts
Growth, inflation, labour market, pay in the private sector
Private firms paying more for IT staff
Nurses and doctors migrating overseas; an ageing population needing more care
Online services replacing paper; new medical technology
Employment law, data protection, health and safety
A change in employment law or service rules
Staffing for hurricane response; energy-saving targets

blocks.p: A **SWOT** analysis sorts findings into **internal** factors (strengths and weaknesses) and **external** factors (opportunities and threats).

head: Factors
Helpful
Harmful
rows: **Strengths:** experienced core staff; a good training unit; staff skilled in data analysis
**Weaknesses:** high vacancy rate in specialist posts; burnout; weak HR data
**Opportunities:** a partnership with a nursing school; a new university programme supplying graduates
**Threats:** overseas recruitment of staff; budget cuts; private firms paying more

blocks.p: The HR objectives then respond to the most important findings, using strengths and opportunities to deal with weaknesses and threats. For example, a hospital might aim to cut the vacancy rate for specialist nurses from 18% to 9% within three years through a training partnership and retention measures, and to cut sickness absence through a wellbeing programme.

blocks.note: A common mistake: putting external things (a threat from overseas recruiters) under weaknesses. Ask: is it inside the organisation's control and part of the organisation (internal), or is it outside (external)?
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Before you can forecast, you must know what you have. Build a **workforce profile** from the HR information system (HRIS) and other records.

head: Item
What it shows
rows: The approved list of posts and grades the body may fill
How many posts are filled and how many are vacant
How many staff are near retirement; the pipeline of younger staff
What skills the body has (see skills audit)
Gender, disability, geographical spread, grade distribution
How staff feel about their work, management and pay

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Staff aged 55 or over ÷ total staff × 100

blocks.p: A **skills audit** finds out which skills staff have now, so they can be compared with the skills the plan needs. Use questionnaires, interviews, appraisal and training records, and managers' input. Record skills by job group and location. The result shows where there are **skills gaps** and where skills are not being used.

An **exit interview** is held with a person who is leaving, to learn why. Patterns (poor management, no development, pay, flexibility) show what to fix. Analyse them by grade, job group and length of service.
A reliable **HRIS** gives accurate data for planning and monitoring: posts, leave, training, ages, grades. Poor data leads to poor plans. Check data quality regularly.

blocks.note: Staff health and family information is sensitive personal data. Collect only what you need for a stated purpose, keep it secure, restrict who can see it and follow the data protection law.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Forecasting demand and supply, and the gap

blocks.h: Demand: how many staff will be needed?

head: Method
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Uses a fixed relationship between workload and staff, such as one inspector per 60 premises
Assumes productivity stays the same; wrong if new technology or procedures change the work
Extends past patterns of staff numbers into the future
Assumes the future is like the past; ignores planned change
Takes account of planned change and local knowledge
May be biased (asking for more than needed)
Experts give anonymous estimates in several rounds until views come together
Reduces bias and the influence of senior voices
Takes time; needs a good facilitator

blocks.p: In practice, use a **mix**: ratios based on forecast workload, adjusted for expected changes (such as an online system), then checked by managers or a panel.

**Worked example (ratio method).** A food-safety unit needs one inspector for every 60 premises. There will be 9,600 premises. Inspectors needed = 9,600 ÷ 60 = **160**. A new mobile inspection app may let each inspector cover more premises, so the planner adjusts the ratio and records the assumption.

blocks.h: Supply: how many staff will be available?

head: Source
Notes
rows: Current staff, adjusted for **retirements, resignations, deaths, promotions out, transfers**. Use age data, turnover history and succession plans.
Graduates from universities and training institutions, skills in the labour market, competition from other employers, migration

blocks.p: **Attrition (wastage)** is the gradual loss of staff through retirement, resignation, or death, especially when posts are not refilled. **Worked example:** in a unit of 80 posts, 6 retire, 4 resign and 2 are promoted out in a year. Posts to refill = 6 + 4 + 2 = 12. As a percentage of the unit: 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = **15%**.
A **gap analysis** compares the forecast demand with the forecast supply, by job group, skill, grade and location. A positive gap is a shortage; a negative gap is a surplus.

**Worked example.** A unit will need 160 staff and has 142 now. Gap = 160 − 142 = 18, **before allowing for leavers**. If 8 leave during the year, the number to recruit = 18 + 8 = **26**. Another agency will need 240 staff next year, has 215, and expects 12 leavers: recruit (240 − 215) + 12 = **37**.

flow: State the demand (number and skills) by job group and year
State the supply from the current workforce, after retirements, resignations and promotions
Subtract: demand − supply = gap
Say whether the gap is a shortage or a surplus, how large, and when it will be felt
Rank the gaps by importance to the corporate goals
Choose the strategies to close them

blocks.note: Always work out the gap **after** expected leavers. A simple 'need minus have' answer forgets that people will leave during the year.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Setting HR objectives and choosing strategies

blocks.p: HR objectives translate the gaps into targets. Make them **SMART**: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**chievable, **R**elevant (linked to the corporate goals), **T**ime-bound.

head: Poor objective
SMART objective
rows: 'Cut the vacancy rate for specialist nurses from 18% to 9% by March 2029.'
'Reduce turnover among IT officers with under five years of service from 22% to 12% within three years.'
'Give every records officer 5 days of digital skills training by the end of year 2.'

head: Strategy
What it includes
Public service points
rows: Attracting and selecting people for gaps; job descriptions; advertising; assessment
Must be **fair, open selection on merit**; follow service rules and approvals
Career paths, training, flexible working, recognition, good management, wellbeing
Pay is set within central policy: seek approval or use other allowed incentives; exit interviews show what to fix
Training needs analysis, induction, leadership programmes, qualifications
Base it on a **training needs analysis** so that training closes the skills gaps found
Identify critical posts, name possible successors, develop a talent pool, knowledge transfer
Needed when many senior or technical officers will retire
Work plans, appraisal, feedback; links individual goals to the plan's aims
Supports fairness in progression and rewards
Workload, support, employee assistance programme, safe work
Needed where surveys show stress and burnout
Accessible recruitment, workplace adjustments, fair treatment
If the profile shows few people with disabilities, plan for access and adjustments
Consultation, grievance and discipline rules, working with unions
Union consultation as agreements and law require
Contracting specialists when needed, temporary staff, shared services, outsourcing
For skills needed only a few months a year
Consultation, retraining and support when roles change
Needed when records clerks move into digital roles, or agencies merge

flow: Identify the posts at risk and when they will fall vacant; rank them by how critical and hard to fill they are
For key posts, name possible successors and assess how ready each is
Develop a **talent pool** through leadership programmes, acting appointments, projects, rotation and coaching
Arrange **knowledge transfer**: mentoring, written procedures and contacts, overlap before retirement; part-time or advisory roles where the rules allow
Prepare open, merit-based external recruitment early where no internal candidate is ready
Keep the developing officers (clear career paths and recognition)
Measure: for example the share of critical posts with a ready successor

blocks.note: If many senior officers will retire soon, the strategy is **succession planning and knowledge transfer**, not simply more recruitment. If staff leave because of workload and stress, the strategy is a **wellbeing** one. Match the strategy to the cause found in the analysis.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Consultation improves the quality of the plan and the chance that it will be carried out. Without it, the plan may rest on wrong assumptions, meet resistance, or fail for lack of funds.

head: Stakeholder
Why involve them
How
rows: Know the strategic goals and the people their units will need
Represent employees; must be engaged on changes to conditions
Bodies that approve budgets and posts
Decide whether proposals can be funded
Engage early, especially on new posts and costs

ul: Map the stakeholders and decide how to involve each one.
Share the draft with clear deadlines for comments.
**Report back** on how views were used, revise the plan, and keep stakeholders informed during implementation.
Cost each action: recruitment, training, retention measures, systems, additional posts.
Include salary and employer contributions for new posts at the current rates.
Work out the cost for each year of the plan.
Compare the total with the budget available.

blocks.p: **Worked example.** A municipal corporation plans to recruit 28 officers at a recruitment cost of J$95,000 each, and to give 2 days of training to each of 200 staff at J$9,000 per person per day.
Another example: training J$7,200,000 for 400 staff is J$7,200,000 ÷ 400 = **J$18,000** per person.

blocks.h: When the plan costs more than the budget

ul: **Rank actions** by impact on the corporate goals and **phase** them over the plan period.
Fill critical posts first; promote or transfer existing staff where possible.
Reduce costs by cutting turnover: every officer retained saves recruitment and induction costs.
Group training to cut the cost per head.
Present the costed case to budget holders and central bodies, and obtain the approvals needed.
Do not simply cut induction or training: poorly prepared staff are more likely to leave.
HR policies that carry out the plan must follow **employment law and service rules**.
Collecting staff data must have a clear purpose and follow the **data protection law**.
The head of the body gives final approval; central bodies approve posts and budgets.

blocks.p: A plan is only useful if it is carried out. The implementation section should contain **actions, owners, timelines, resources and measures**.

head: Action
Owner
Start
Finish
Resource
Measure
rows: Launch a leadership development programme for 20 officers
Share of critical posts with a ready successor

blocks.p: A **Gantt chart** shows the timing of each action over the plan period as bars along a time scale, so overlaps and delays can be seen.

head: Risk
Response
rows: Budgets cut or posts not approved
Cost every action; rank by impact; engage approving bodies early; have a phased fallback
Forecasts wrong (for example more staff leave than expected)
Monitor turnover and exit reasons; plan scenarios
Give each director ownership of relevant actions; report progress to the senior team
Data quality checks; improve the HRIS
Change in government policy (such as a merger)
Review the plan at least yearly, and immediately when major change is announced
Key staff leaving faster than forecast
Retention measures; succession plan; early warning from turnover data

blocks.p: Record risks in a **risk register** with owners and responses.

head: Area
Measures
rows: Vacancy rate; average time to fill; share of critical posts with a ready successor
Turnover (overall and for key groups such as IT officers); exit interview reasons
Training days per officer; completion rate; whether training closed the skills gaps
Share of officers with agreed work plans; yearly staff survey
Absence rate; use of the employee assistance programme

ul: Each objective needs at least one measure with a **baseline**, a **target** and a **date**.
Take data from the HRIS, checked for accuracy.

Report **regularly** (for example each quarter) to senior management on a one-page dashboard with measures against target, red, amber and green status, and a short explanation and action for any measure off track. Give a fuller report each year.

blocks.p: When the plan has been approved, brief staff on **what it means for them**: what is changing, when, how it affects jobs, training and career, and where to ask questions. Brief managers first. Where roles will change (for example records clerks moving into digital roles), include consultation, retraining and support.

ul: **Review at least yearly**, and **immediately** when something major changes: for example, the government announces that two agencies will merge. Update the forecasts, gaps, objectives and costs.
At the end of the plan period, evaluate: **were the HR objectives met, and did they help the organisation reach its goals?** Use the findings in the next plan.
Use the evaluation to learn which strategies worked and which did not.

blocks.note: Report to senior management on measures, not activity. 'We held ten training sessions' is activity. 'Share of critical posts with a ready successor rose from 20% to 55%' is a result.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: state the purpose of an HR strategic plan and say how it links to the corporate plan and covers the same period;
explain the difference between strategic and day-to-day HR issues;
carry out an environmental scan with PESTLE and sort findings into a SWOT;
build a workforce profile and calculate vacancy rate, turnover, age profile, absence rate and average time to fill;
explain a skills audit, exit interviews and the HR information system;
forecast demand using the ratio method, trends, managerial judgement and the Delphi technique;
forecast supply allowing for retirements, resignations and promotions;
do a gap analysis and work out the number to recruit after leavers;
write SMART HR objectives linked to the corporate goals;
choose strategies for recruitment on merit, retention, development, succession, performance, wellbeing, inclusion, employee relations, flexible resourcing and change;
consult stakeholders and explain why;
cost a plan, compare it with the budget and deal with a shortfall;
write an implementation plan with actions, owners, timelines, resources and measures;
manage risks with a risk register;
report progress quarterly and review the plan yearly and when major change is announced.

terms: A plan for having the right people, with the right skills, in the right places and at the right cost to achieve the organisation's goals
The organisation's plan of goals, from which the HR plan is built
A study of outside changes that may affect the workforce
Political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors
The approved list of posts, with their grades, that a public body may fill
Gradual loss of staff through retirement, resignation or death
A review of the skills staff have now
A meeting with a leaving employee to learn why they are going
Human resource information system: stores staff data such as posts, leave and training
An estimate of the number of staff, and skills, that will be needed
An estimate of the staff who will be available
Comparing forecast demand and supply to find shortages or surpluses
Forecasting using a fixed relationship between workload and staff
Experts give anonymous estimates in rounds until their views come together
Preparing people to fill key posts when they fall vacant
A group of staff with the potential to fill key posts in future, being developed for them
The planned passing of skills and know-how from experienced officers to newer ones
A study of the skills gap that training must close
A bar chart showing the timing of actions over a period
A record of risks, owners and responses

c1.title: A regional health authority in Manchester
c1.text: A regional health authority in Manchester has an approved establishment of 320 nursing posts, of which 40 are vacant. The authority's strategic plan includes opening three community clinics in the next three years. Nurses are being recruited by overseas agencies, and a local nursing school plans to double its graduates. A staff survey shows burnout among the specialist nurses. The HR director is formulating the authority's HR strategic plan.

c2.title: A food-safety unit in a municipal corporation in Clarendon
c2.text: A food-safety unit in a municipal corporation in Clarendon needs one inspector for every 60 food premises. By the end of the plan period there will be 9,600 premises. The unit has 142 inspectors and expects 8 to leave during the year. A mobile inspection app that may let each inspector cover more premises is being tested. The planner has only past staffing numbers and the managers' own estimates to use.

c3.title: Retirements at a statutory body in Portland
c3.text: A statutory body in Portland has 90 senior and technical officers. Thirty of them will reach retirement age within five years, and several hold the only copy of important know-how on how the body's systems work. The body's rules require fair, open selection on merit for any appointment. The HR manager is writing the succession part of the HR strategic plan.

c4.title: Costing and risk in a municipal corporation in St James
c4.text: A municipal corporation in St James plans to recruit 28 officers at a recruitment cost of J$95,000 each, and to give 2 days of training to each of 200 staff at J$9,000 per person per day. The budget available for these two items is J$5,000,000. The new posts must be approved by a central body, which has not yet replied.

c5.title: Monitoring an HR plan in a ministry in Kingston
c5.text: A ministry in Kingston is halfway through a three-year HR plan. Five vacancies this year took 55, 70, 40, 85 and 60 days to fill. The ministry's 150 officers each had 240 working days available and 2,160 days were lost to absence. The government announces that the ministry will merge with a department of another ministry. Senior managers ask for a short quarterly report.

questions.q: Which tool groups outside factors under political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental headings?
o: Skills audit
Gap analysis
PESTLE analysis
Gantt chart
questions.why: PESTLE is the checklist for an environmental scan. A skills audit looks at skills inside the organisation, a gap analysis compares demand and supply, and a Gantt chart shows the timing of actions.

questions.q: In a SWOT analysis, how should the recruitment of nurses by overseas agencies be classed?
o: A threat, since it comes from outside and may reduce the authority's staff
A weakness, since it is a problem the authority has within its control
A strength, since nurses are being trained to a standard that overseas employers value
An opportunity, since fewer nurses will mean lower salary costs
questions.why: Factors outside the organisation are opportunities or threats. Overseas recruitment can reduce the authority's staff, so it is a threat. Weaknesses are internal, such as burnout or high vacancy rates.

questions.q: What is the vacancy rate of the nursing establishment?
questions.why: Vacancy rate = vacant posts / establishment x 100 = 40 / 320 x 100 = 12.5%. The figure 87.5% is the share of posts that are filled.

questions.q: The strategic plan includes three new community clinics. What should the HR director do first?
o: Advertise for nurses for the clinics before the details are agreed with the board
Work out the staff and skills the clinics need and compare with current staff
Wait until the clinics have opened and then see how many staff are really needed
Copy the staffing numbers from another health authority's published plan
questions.why: The HR plan starts from the corporate goal: what people and skills does it need? Demand is forecast, supply is estimated, and the gap shows what to do. Advertising early or copying another plan skips the analysis.

questions.q: Using the ratio method, how many inspectors will the unit need for 9,600 premises?
questions.why: Inspectors needed = 9,600 / 60 = 160. The ratio is one inspector for every 60 premises, so you divide the premises by 60.

questions.q: How many inspectors must the unit recruit, allowing for the 8 who are expected to leave?
questions.why: The gap is 160 - 142 = 18. Eight more are expected to leave, so recruitment must be 18 + 8 = 26. Forgetting the leavers would leave the unit short.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of the ratio method for this unit?
o: It assumes the same premises per inspector, but the app may change this
It cannot be used unless a panel of experts agrees on the ratio
It depends on past staffing numbers, which this unit does not have
It always gives a figure that is higher than the number of staff needed
questions.why: The ratio method assumes productivity stays the same. A new tool may change how many premises one inspector can cover, so the planner should adjust the ratio and record the assumption.

questions.q: The planner has only past staffing numbers. What is the main weakness of trend analysis alone?
o: It is too complicated to use without special computer software or training
It always gives a lower number of staff than the ratio method does
It assumes the past will repeat and ignores planned change, such as the app
It depends on the opinions of managers, who may ask for too many staff
questions.why: Trend analysis extends the past into the future. It does not take account of planned changes such as new technology or a larger workload, so it is best used with other methods.

questions.q: What percentage of the senior and technical officers will reach retirement age within five years?
questions.why: Percentage = 30 / 90 x 100 = 33.3%. This is one-third of the group, which is a serious succession risk. The figure 66.7% is the share that will not retire.

questions.q: What should the HR manager do first in the succession plan?
o: Identify the posts that will fall vacant, and rank them by how critical they are
Appoint an external replacement for every officer who will retire this year
Offer every officer in the body a leadership course during the first year
Ask the retiring officers to choose their own successors from the staff
questions.why: Succession planning starts by finding the posts at risk and ranking them. Effort and money are then put where the risk is highest. Choosing successors without assessment, or treating every post alike, wastes resources.

questions.q: Several retiring officers hold know-how that is not written down. Which action fits best?
o: Let them retire on the usual date, since they are leaving anyway
Pay them a one-time bonus when they retire to thank them
Recruit external staff and tell them to rebuild the knowledge
Arrange mentoring, written procedures and an overlap period before they leave
questions.why: Knowledge transfer is the planned passing of know-how from experienced officers to others. Mentoring, written procedures and a handover period protect the body from losing key knowledge.

questions.q: No internal candidate is ready for one key post. What should the plan provide for?
o: Appointing the most senior internal officer to the post without any process
Early, open external recruitment on merit, so the post is not left empty
Advertising the post only inside the body so that it can be filled quickly
Leaving the post vacant until an internal candidate becomes ready
questions.why: Recruitment into the public service must be fair, open and on merit. Starting early avoids leaving critical posts empty. Appointing without a process or restricting the advertisement would not meet service rules.

questions.q: What is the total recruitment cost?
questions.why: Recruitment cost = 28 x J$95,000 = J$2,660,000. J$3,600,000 is the training cost, not the recruitment cost.

questions.q: What is the total training cost?
questions.why: Training days = 200 staff x 2 days = 400 days. Cost = 400 x J$9,000 = J$3,600,000. Taking one day only would give J$1,800,000.

questions.q: By how much do the two items exceed the J$5,000,000 budget?
The central body has not yet approved the 28 posts. How should this be handled in the plan?
o: Ignore it, since the posts are in the corporate plan and approval is certain
Recruit all 28 officers now and ask for approval after they have started
Record it as a risk, engage the body early and plan a phased fallback
Remove the 28 posts from the plan and give the work to existing staff
questions.why: Lack of approval is a funding risk. The plan should name it, get the approving bodies involved early and have a phased fallback. Recruiting without approval, or dropping the posts, would not meet the organisation's goals.

questions.q: How many days longer than the average did the slowest of the five vacancies take to fill?
o: 30 days
85 days
23 days
15 days
questions.why: Average = (55 + 70 + 40 + 85 + 60) / 5 = 310 / 5 = 62 days. The slowest took 85 days, which is 85 - 62 = 23 days longer than the average.

questions.q: What was the absence rate?
questions.why: Days available = 150 x 240 = 36,000. Absence rate = 2,160 / 36,000 x 100 = 6%. The figure 94% is the share of days that were worked.

questions.q: Which format best suits the quarterly report for senior managers?
o: A full list of every training session held in the quarter, in date order
A copy of the HRIS records for every officer in the ministry
A verbal summary given at the start of a meeting, with no figures
A one-page dashboard of measures against target with RAG status and notes
questions.why: Senior managers need a short, regular report showing results against targets, with exceptions flagged and actions noted. A list of activity or raw records does not show whether the plan is working.

questions.q: Which information is most useful for forecasting the external supply of skilled staff?
o: The age profile of the people already working in the organisation
Graduate output of training institutions and labour-market trends
Reasons given by leavers in exit interviews held last year
The number of days lost to absence in each department last year
questions.why: External supply is the pool of people outside the organisation: graduates, people in the labour market and what other employers are doing. Age profile, exit interviews and absence records describe the existing workforce, which is the internal supply.
